Hi Cyracen,
The cord brought us closer this year. That sentence sounds so obviously digital-age that it almost embarrasses me to write it, but there’s no other way to say it honestly. We met through Discord servers: mutual friends, overlapping interests. And then, over months of messages and voice calls and the ambient awareness of each other’s presence, something accumulated that I’d have to call friendship.
McLuhan’s line about the medium being the message gets quoted so often it’s almost lost its meaning, but I think about it whenever I try to explain how online relationships work to people who haven’t had them.1 Text flattens tone but preserves exactness. Voice adds warmth but disappears the moment it’s spoken. The rhythm of when someone shows up (which threads they join, which they ignore, how long they take to respond) becomes its own form of communication. You learn someone through the gaps between messages as much as the messages themselves.
What’s funny is how “online” all of this sounds, and how unavoidably real it becomes anyway. Sherry Turkle wrote about digital connection as a thin substitute for the real thing, “alone together.”2 I don’t think that’s wrong, exactly. Some online friendships stay thin. Others don’t. The difference, I think, is whether people are willing to be awkward and show up even when there’s nothing clever to contribute. You do that consistently.

What I respect most is how you carry yourself in a chat. Your tone doesn’t drift into the cheap cynicism that’s basically the default register of the internet. You don’t treat conversation like a game of status, where every message is really about positioning. You say what you think, and you listen to what other people think.
And when you do talk about things you care about, it lands differently than most people’s opinions: less “here’s my take,” more “here’s what survived contact with reality.” You can tell the thinking happened before the speaking, that you’re reporting back from somewhere you’ve already been. The medium didn’t make you honest, but it did make your honesty visible.

I’m glad we got to know each other this year. It happened slowly, without any single moment you could point to, just the gradual accumulation of shared context and mutual respect. And I’m looking forward to whatever the next year turns into: more messages, more voice, more “prompts in the bags” meme.

marshall mcluhan, understanding media (1964), chapter 1, “the medium is the message.” the core insight: technologies reshape how we think, perceive, and relate to each other, whatever content they carry. ↩


sherry turkle, alone together: why we expect more from technology and less from each other (2011). a skeptical take on digital intimacy, the argument that we’re substituting connection-lite for the real thing. i think she’s half right. ↩
